pool.q: In marketing, what creates value for the customer?
options: A product with its perceived attributes and benefits
pool.explain: A product can be a good, a service or an idea.
pool.evidence: In marketing, a product (a good, service, or idea), along with its perceived attributes and benefits, creates value for the customer.

pool.q: Which is an example of an intangible product attribute?
pool.explain: Intangible attributes are symbolic.
pool.evidence: Intangible attributes are symbolic, such as brand image.

pool.q: What does someone buying a plane ride mainly want?
options: The benefit of a quick way to get from one city to another
pool.explain: Products deliver benefits through tangible and intangible parts.
pool.evidence: The person who buys a plane ride on United Airlines is looking for a quick way to get from one city to another (the benefit).

pool.q: Why are new products important to companies?
options: They pump life into sales, helping the firm survive and grow
pool.explain: Many firms get most of their profits from new products.
pool.evidence: New products pump life into company sales, enabling the firm not only to survive but also to grow.

pool.q: How high can new-product failure rates be for household and grocery products?
pool.explain: Developing new products is costly and risky.
pool.evidence: New-product failure rates for household and grocery products can approach 80 percent.

pool.q: How are new-product goals usually stated?
pool.explain: Setting goals is the first step in developing new products.
pool.evidence: Set new-product goals: New-product goals are usually stated as financial objectives.

pool.q: When is a product classified as a new product?
options: When it gets new packaging only
When it has a new brand name and is in a product category new to the organisation
When it is sold in a new shop
pool.explain: Service firms also develop new services.
pool.evidence: When a firm introduces a product that has a new brand name and is in a product category new to the organization, it is classified as a new product.

pool.q: What is the product life cycle?
options: The time it takes to manufacture one item
A pattern of sales and profits over time for a product or product category
pool.explain: Firms keep revising the marketing mix through the stages.
pool.evidence: The product life cycle is a pattern of sales and profits over time for a product (Ivory dishwashing liquid) or a product category (liquid detergents).

pool.q: What usually happens to profits in the introduction stage?
options: They are usually small or negative
They are guaranteed by the government
pool.explain: Costs are high and sales volume is low.
pool.evidence: Hence, profits are usually small or negative.

pool.q: What characterises the growth stage?
options: Sales grow at an increasing rate, profits are healthy and competitors enter
pool.explain: Distribution becomes a key to success.
pool.evidence: In this stage, sales grow at an increasing rate, profits are healthy, and many competitors enter the market.

pool.q: Why focus on the user and their problem rather than a particular solution?
options: Because users always know the solution
You often learn unexpected things about their needs, and the real problem may differ
pool.explain: The real problem might not be the one you first thought.
pool.evidence: Focusing on the user and the problem they’re trying to solve - rather than a particular solution - often means that you learn unexpected things about their needs.

pool.q: What is a risk of trying to solve a whole problem for users?
options: Building big, complicated services that try to do too much
pool.explain: Services should join up without becoming unintuitive.
pool.evidence: However we should be careful not to build big, complicated services that are not intuitive to use because they try to do too much.

pool.q: When trying to understand users, what context should you look at?
options: Only the screen they are using
The full context of what the user is trying to achieve, not just their interaction with you
Only what managers think users want
pool.explain: Users' goals extend beyond your service.
pool.evidence: Look at the full context to understand what the user is trying to achieve, not just the part where they have to interact with government.

pool.q: What must you understand before committing to build a service?
options: The problem that needs to be solved
The list of features competitors have
pool.explain: That is the purpose of discovery.
pool.evidence: Before you commit to building a service, you need to understand the problem that needs to be solved.

pool.q: Should you start building your service in discovery?
pool.explain: Discovery is for understanding the problem.
pool.evidence: You should not start building your service in discovery.

pool.q: What does running an alpha mean you have decided?
options: That the benefits of looking further into the problem outweigh the cost
pool.explain: What you learn in discovery decides whether to move to alpha.
pool.evidence: Running an alpha means you’ve decided that the benefits of looking further into the problem outweigh the cost.

pool.q: What should what you learn in discovery help you decide?
options: The final price of the product
Whether to move forward to the alpha phase
pool.explain: Discovery informs the go/no-go decision for alpha.
pool.evidence: What you learn during discovery should help you work out whether you want to move forward to the alpha phase.

pool.q: What is the alpha phase for?
options: Trying out different solutions to the problems learnt about in discovery
pool.explain: Spend alpha building prototypes and testing ideas.
pool.evidence: Alpha is where you try out different solutions to the problems you learnt about during discovery.

pool.q: Why might you prototype only the most challenging areas in alpha?
options: To do the minimum needed to test your riskiest assumptions
Because the whole journey is always easy
pool.explain: You don't have to prototype the entire journey.
pool.evidence: This lets you do the minimum you need to test your riskiest assumptions.

pool.q: What does the guidance say alpha is a chance to do?
options: Explore new approaches and challenge the way things are done
pool.explain: Don't be afraid to challenge current ways of working.
pool.evidence: And do not be afraid to challenge the way things are done at the moment: alpha is a chance to explore new approaches.

pool.q: What happens in the beta phase?
options: You research the problem for the first time
You take your best idea from alpha and start building it for real
pool.explain: Beta has private and public stages.
pool.evidence: The beta phase is where you take your best idea from alpha and start building it for real.

pool.q: How does private beta start?
options: By opening the service to everyone
By inviting a limited number of people to use your service
By shutting down the alpha team
pool.explain: This is to get feedback and make improvements.
pool.evidence: You’ll start in private beta by inviting a limited number of people to use your service.

pool.q: What are the two stages of beta?
pool.explain: A beta assessment moves you into public beta.
pool.evidence: The stages of beta There are 2 stages to beta: private and public.

pool.q: What is the live phase about?
options: Supporting the service sustainably and continuing to iterate and improve
pool.explain: Improvement continues after launch.
pool.evidence: The live phase is about supporting the service in a sustainable way, and continuing to iterate and make improvements.

pool.q: What should you spend public beta doing?
pool.explain: Work out continuous improvement and team needs.
pool.evidence: Spend public beta preparing for live.

pool.q: What is a multidisciplinary team?
options: A team with people doing a variety of different roles
A team that works in several countries
pool.explain: Roles include product manager, service owner, delivery manager and more.
pool.evidence: Your service team must include people doing a variety of different roles (this type of team is called a multidisciplinary team).

pool.q: Which of these is part of the product manager's job?
options: Prioritise user stories for each work sprint
pool.explain: Removing blockers is the delivery manager's job.
pool.evidence: prioritise user stories for each work sprint

pool.q: What is the 'product vision'?
options: The future goal of the service, defined by the product manager
A camera used for product photos
pool.explain: It comes from agile project management.
pool.evidence: define what the future goal of the service is (often called the ‘product vision’ in agile project management )

pool.q: Who sets up the agile environment and removes blockers?
pool.explain: The delivery manager also helps the team self-organise.
pool.evidence: Your delivery manager is responsible for: setting up the agile environment your team needs to build and iterate a user-centred service removing obstacles or ‘blockers’ to progress

pool.q: What is one-to-one marketing?
options: Creating a customised marketing mix for each consumer
pool.explain: It is a significant trend in products and pricing.
pool.evidence: Another significant trend is the use of one-to-one marketing to create a customized marketing mix for each consumer.

pool.q: How has internet technology changed buyers' position?
options: Buyers have less information than before
Buyers can quickly compare products and prices, improving their bargaining position
Buyers must visit stores in person
pool.explain: Sellers also collect detailed data to tailor products and prices.
pool.evidence: This link is enabling buyers to quickly and easily compare products and prices, putting them in a better bargaining position.

pool.q: What does technology let sellers collect to tailor products and prices?
options: Detailed data about customers' buying habits, preferences and spending limits
pool.explain: Data enables tailored products and prices.
pool.evidence: At the same time, the technology enables sellers to collect detailed data about customers’ buying habits, preferences, and even spending limits so that they can tailor their products and prices.
